title: Mira's songs today
hookLine: her songs are still sung across India
tomorrow: a poet's notebook left on a London train. what was inside?

lines: HOW WE KNOW, AND WHY WE CAN'T.
cards: Rappers drop their own names into a verse. Mira's songs do something like it. The songs credited to her close on a signature line: Mira ke prabhu Giridhar Nagar, Mira's lord is Giridhar, the clever one.
The poet signs her name inside the poem, like a seal pressed into wax at the bottom of a letter. Here's the puzzle. That signature is how we know a song is Mira's.
It's also the reason nobody can be sure it is.

teach.b: Scholars call that closing signature the chhap, a stamp. In north Indian devotional song, a poet set their name into the last verse.
But a stamp can be borrowed. John Stratton Hawley, who has studied the old manuscripts, finds that only some of the songs sung as Mira's reach back to early copies.
The rest grew as people sang: someone singing in Mira's spirit made a new song and gave it her name, the way you might sign a card for the whole family.

teach.h: SUNG AS ONE OF THEIR OWN.
teach.b: Parita Mukta listened to village singers in Rajasthan and found communities who sing Mira as one of their own, with songs no palace ever heard, sung at night gatherings in their own dialect.
To them she is not a distant queen. So who wrote them? Mira, and the people who kept singing her.
And that's bhakti again. A bhajan isn't a museum piece. It belongs to whoever sings it to God.
Singing groups called bhajan mandalis meet in homes and temples and pass these songs voice to voice, and one line sung under her name sounds like a vow: mere to Giridhar Gopal, dusro na koi.
My own is Giridhar Gopal, no one else.
Whoever first sang it, that line is alive because people keep singing it. The mystery of who wrote it doesn't weaken the song. It's how the song survived.

how: Mira's bhajans are sung in temples, in homes and by village and neighborhood singing groups (bhajan mandalis), as well as by classical and film singers; the last verse usually carries her signature line naming Giridhar.

games.q: a family recipe card says 'Aunt Rose's,' but three generations have changed it since. a cousin says it isn't really Rose's anymore. what fits how Mira's songs live?
o: it's still Rose's, and everyone's now: it's alive because people keep making it.
it stopped being Rose's the moment anyone changed a single thing in it.
it belongs to nobody now, so her name should come off the card.
games.why: songs in Mira's name grew as singers sang them. the signature stayed, and the singing kept her alive.

practice: If you can, play one recording of a Mira bhajan, any singer, and listen for the end, where her name comes in. If not, hum the last line of a song someone once taught you.
For two minutes, let that closing line be the one that stays.

wordCard.voice: Mira's songs today: bhajans sung under her name, some from her and some from singers who came after, kept alive by being sung together, in homes, temples and village courtyards.

orig.note: Hindi and Sanskrit: a devotional song, sung to God, often together. Mira's songs are sung as bhajans.

carryVoice: Keep this one: still sung, from voice to voice, and signed with her name. Two days with Mira, done.
